Kenneth wants to choose between fix options before code is written: first deliverable is a short options write-up (untracked file in the worktree root, never committed), then stop and wait. Task:
Problem: after a MakerWorld 3MF with an embedded profile has been open, opening a plain STL as a new project starts its chat with nine edit rows before anything else, all attributed to the person: "Sparse infill density 20% → 15% · you, in 0.20mm Standard @BBL A1M · 05:56", "Sparse infill pattern Cross Zag → Cross Hatch", "Type Normal (auto) → Tree (auto)", "First layer 0.36 mm → 0.5 mm", "Inherits profile 0.20mm Standard @BBL A1M → Empty", "print_settings_id HSW_Kabelhalter → Empty", and so on. They are the previous project's embedded preset values being reset to the system preset when the old project is released and the new one starts. The person sees raw setting keys, a designer's preset name from a file they closed, the word "you" on changes they never made, and cannot tell whether anything is wrong. Frame 1B-02 of the critique shows it.

Task, in this order:
1. Reproduce it in the real app (recipe in the background notes) and trace where the rows come from: the host edit feed (`WorkspaceEditHub` and whatever publishes preset diffs to the page) and the page's edit-row rendering in `MessageList`. Establish exactly which transition emits them (project release, preset reset, new project load) and why they are tagged as the person's and land in the new chat's timeline, and whether the same rows appear when a file is opened from Finder or dropped.
2. Write an untracked options note (`phantom-edits-options.md` in the worktree root) with two to four options, each with what the person sees afterwards, where the change lives (host or page, per the page-first rule in `agent-docs/jusprin/architecture.md`), and a recommendation. Candidates: suppress edit reporting during project release and open; attribute those edits to the file or the app and collapse them to one line such as "Settings from universal_cable_holder_v2.3mf were put back"; keep the rows but only in the old project's chat. Also say whether keys like `print_settings_id` and values like "Empty" should ever reach a row.
3. Stop and wait for Kenneth to choose. Do not implement before he answers.

Done, after his choice, means: opening a new project after a 3MF with embedded settings draws no rows attributed to the person; a test covers the transition (the existing edit-feed tests are the place to look); verified in the real app with a screenshot of the new project's chat.

name: live-test-built-app-on-mac
description: "How to launch, see, and drive the locally built JusPrin app on the Mac: the shared bundle id binds tools to the wrong instance, and \"on another Space\" usually means the window is on the second monitor, not that the user is in full screen."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: fa2d66ed-e217-440b-aae0-da4164953edc
  modified: 2026-09-23T18:10:30.736Z
---

Every build of the fork (and /Applications/OrcaSlicer.app) shares bundle id `com.softfever3d.orca-slicer`. The desktop-control tools resolve an app by bundle id and bind to whichever instance comes first, so `app_list_windows` returns `[]` and filtered screenshots hide the window you actually launched.

**Working recipe (2026-09-05):** `ditto` the built .app into the scratchpad, `plutil -replace CFBundleIdentifier -string com.jusprin.worktree-test`, `codesign --force --deep -s -`, then `open -n <copy>.app --args <model>` and `request_access` for the new id. `app_screenshot`/`app_click` then work and include popup menus. A display-scope `left_click` on the header did NOT open the fork's PopupWindow menus, but a background `app_click` did; take the pixel-level `zoom` with the display tools afterwards (call `app_release` first). Display-scope `Escape` does not close those popups; a click elsewhere does.

The MCP discovery file `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/jusprin/mcp.json` points at the newest instance's `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp`; `tests/mcp/probe.py`'s `call()` can drive real tools (e.g. `workspace_inspect`, then `report_slice_review` with sessionId/plateId/sliceResultId) to put the header into the Check-print state without lldb. lldb `expr` cannot call inline accessors like `status_row()`.

**Why:** On 2026-09-01 a verification pass screenshotted the stock app instead of the build; on 2026-09-05 the tools bound to another session's main-repo build.

**How to apply:** Confirm the pid with `pgrep -fl OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS`; never kill an instance you did not launch. `osascript` System Events by unix id still works to set `frontmost`. See [[jusprin-shell-phase-1-design]] and [[orca-inherited-teardown-crash]].

**"On another Space" usually means "on the other monitor."** Cost about ten turns on
2026-09-09 and produced a wrong report to Kenneth. `app_list_windows` returns
`is_off_space: true` and clicks are refused with "this window is on another Space";
`app_bring_to_current_space` then fails with "the user's current Space is a full-screen
app." Both messages are about Spaces, so the natural read is that the user is sitting in
a full-screen app — but with *Displays have separate Spaces* on, a window merely sitting
on the second monitor produces exactly the same symptoms. Kenneth was not in full screen;
the harness had opened on the Acer.

Tell them apart before saying anything to the user: take a **display-scope** screenshot
(`app_release`, then `computer_batch` screenshot). Its header names the monitor it
captured and lists the others — if the window shows up there, it is a monitor problem,
not a Space problem, and the display-scope tools can drive it immediately. Never conclude
"the user is in a full-screen app" from the background tools' error text alone.

The same flag also flaps: a window can read `is_off_space: false` and click fine, then
read `true` a minute later. Clicks delivered while it is true report `ok ... unverified`
and silently do nothing. **A click that reports "unverified" and changes nothing is not
evidence of an application bug** — on 2026-09-09 that nearly became a filed defect about
being unable to retry after a failed MCP connect. Re-verify on a reachable window before
concluding anything about the app.

**Prefer the shell harness over a re-signed app copy for Agent-panel work.**
`tests/shell/.../JusPrinShellHarness.app` already carries its own bundle id
(`io.jusprin.shell-harness`), so none of the bundle-id collision above applies, and
`--manual-unconfigured` lands directly on the dock's not-set-up state — one click from
the Agent setup chooser. Build target is `shell_integration_harness`, not `shell_harness`.

**Isolate `$HOME` when testing MCP client setup.** `Mcp::default_catalog_paths()` reads
`$HOME`, so the flow will happily rewrite the real `~/.cursor/mcp.json`. Launch with
`HOME=<scratch>` holding a `.cursor/mcp.json` fixture; detection, the diff, and the write
all follow it. Force a write failure with `chmod 444` on the file **and** `555` on its
directory — the directory alone is not enough.

**Re-signed copies trigger system prompts.** Each rebuild + ad-hoc re-sign changes the cdhash, so macOS re-asks for Downloads access (recent-project thumbnail load blocks in `fopen`) and Keychain access (agent runtime reads the API key). Both are prompts only the user can answer. Avoid them by running the binary directly (`nohup <copy>.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer --datadir <scratch copy of JusPrin2 with recent_projects cleared> <model>`) with `OPENAI_API_KEY=<placeholder>` in the environment, which short-circuits the Keychain lookup in `AgentConfiguration.cpp`. Use `sample <pid>` on the main thread to see which prompt is blocking.

**Stale as of 2026-09-18 (branch claude/printer-conversation-panel-af11cb):** `load_agent_runtime` reads the key only from app config (`jusprin_agent` / `openai_api_key`); no env var or Keychain lookup exists there. In the shell harness, `OPENAI_API_KEY` only feeds the docked pane via `install_harness_agent`; the printer panel builds its own runtime from app config, so `--printer-live` writes the key into the run's throwaway conf. Pass it as `std::string`: `AppConfig::set(section, key, const char*)` silently picks the `bool` overload and stores `true` (seen as a 401 "key rejected"). The harness temp data dir then holds the real key: delete `/var/folders/*/*/T/jusprin-shell-*` dirs from those runs afterwards.

**Hands-on printer panel with a live model (2026-09-23, jusprin-newui, uncommitted at the time):** `--manual-live-agent` now also writes `OPENAI_API_KEY` into the run's app config, so Home → "+ Add printer" gets a live printer chat. Feed the key from `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/JusPrin2.conf` (`jusprin_agent.openai_api_key`) via env without echoing it. Drive it with display-scope `computer_batch` clicks/typing (background `app_click` does nothing on the web view). The scripted `--printer-live` run hangs when the model doesn't pick the printer its next "tap" step expects; kill it. Afterwards `rm -rf` the run's `/var/folders/*/*/T/jusprin-shell-*` dir — killed runs leave it behind with the key.

**Give each automated harness run a fresh scratch `$HOME`.** On 2026-09-09 a second run
against a reused scratch `$HOME` (and with a `jusprin-mcp` helper left over from the
first) never got past the Agent page handshake: it printed `HARNESS WAIT
agent_bridge_handshake preview=0 plate=0 slice_valid=1` about twice a second forever and
had to be killed at ten minutes. Runs before and after it, each with a freshly created
`$HOME` and a `pkill -f jusprin-mcp` first, finished with zero `HARNESS WAIT` lines at
all. **The cause was not isolated** — reuse and the stale helper were not separated, so
treat this as a recipe, not an explanation. `rm -rf` and recreate the scratch `$HOME`,
`pkill -f jusprin-mcp`, then run; if the handshake wait appears anyway, kill it early
rather than assuming the change under test broke the bridge.

**2026-09-19 addendum:** background `app_click` on the Home/Agent WKWebViews reports
"ok … unverified" and nothing happens; only display-scope `computer_batch` clicks
reach the page. The re-signed copy opened on the *Built-in Retina Display* while the
display tools default to the Acer, so `switch_display` first. `Return` in the composer
sends in the real app; in the built-in-browser fixture it does not (click the send
button). Another Claude session holding the computer-use lock blocks `request_access`
until Kenneth stops that session. Page-only states are cheaper via [[fake-host-page-fixture]].

**2026-10-28: background clicks no longer open header popups.** In `--manual`, background `app_click` on the printer chip (body or chevron) left the chip pressed but no menu appeared, and `--printer-menu-capture`'s screen blit came back solid black with the screen unlocked (likely a rebuilt binary losing screen-recording permission). When the Mac screen is locked (`ioreg -n Root -d1 | grep CGSSessionScreenIsLocked`), the computer-use MCP request is auto-denied, `screencapture` fails, and System Events sees zero windows. #### Where logic goes: the page first

When the same logic could live either in C++ or in a React page, put it in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++. The page is quicker to change: Vite hot-reloads it, while a C++ change means relinking a multi-gigabyte GUI library. The page's tests run in milliseconds under Vitest. The text people read is already written in the page. The text the model reads belongs there too.

Strong reasons for C++:

- **It reads or changes OrcaSlicer state:** presets, the model, plates, slicing, the device list. The page never owns project state (see the constraints below).
- **The app has to guarantee it.** This covers what a tool accepts and refuses, which tools a session may call, and what is sent to the model provider (API keys, access codes, project data). Page code can describe a limit, but only the app can enforce one.
- **It has to work without a page:** the MCP server, background work, tests that run without a browser.
- **It needs a thread the page does not have, or has to stay alive at times when the page is not.**

The printer panel shows how this works. The app sends the page only facts: sizes, spools, which printer a card shows, and what a change altered. The page turns those facts into all of the text:

- The page writes the model's instructions in `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` and sends them to the app with `printer_instructions`.
- The page writes the panel's own text in `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts`. That is the opening line and the note that goes with each tap. The opening line is sent with `printer_opening`. The note for a tap is sent inside that tap's payload.

The app's part:

- It decides which tools the model gets: the five printer tools and the four settings tools, the same list in every mode.
- It checks every tool call.
- It refuses a call that does not fit the conversation. Examples are adding a printer outside an Add conversation, changing a printer other than the one the conversation is about, and changing a setting on anything other than that printer.
- It refuses a turn that arrives with no instructions. The app has no prompt of its own to fall back on.
- It posts the opening line once per session.
- It posts the note for a tap only when the tap goes through, and limits the note to 2 KB.
- It still writes the notes for things only the app can find out when the tap arrives: the network printer has gone, the printer's model id is not on the list, or a save or an undo failed.

The project assistant works the same way. Its whole system prompt is written in `AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts`, and `projectInstructions.test.ts` pins it to a fixture so that a change to it is always deliberate. The page sends it with `project_instructions` on every connection. The app keeps it in the project session's profile and sends it, unchanged, as the instructions of every project request; the provider's prompt cache depends on the text staying byte-identical. The app has no default text. A turn the app starts itself before the page has sent the prompt (the first message after a file opens, or Ask AI on a print issue, while the page is still loading) waits in the reply queue and starts when the prompt arrives. The prompt lived in C++ until 2026-10-14 so that the MCP server's instructions could share part of it; they stopped sharing it on 2026-10-10. The MCP server's own instructions (`Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp`) and the request that names a conversation stay in C++: MCP has no page, and the title request is the app's own.

Windows uses WebView2, macOS uses WKWebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. The way the page's files are packaged must work on all three. The prototype packed the whole page into a single local file, because WKWebView failed to load additional files referenced through `file:` URLs. Production keeps the single-file approach, and CMake now builds that file from the TypeScript/React sources.

MCP (Model Context Protocol, which lets external AI tools call the app) and wider agent autonomy are layers that come after this one. They must go through the same typed workspace interface. They must not change who owns the 3D view.

# Phantom "you" edit rows when a file opens as a new project — options

Untracked working note, 2026-10-28. Build: jusprin-newui a684aee37d. Critique frame 1B-02.

## What happens

Reproduced in a scratch copy of the built app (own `--datadir`, `local_machines` emptied). With
`Tape_4_3MF.3mf` open (a MakerWorld file whose embedded process preset differs from
"0.20mm Standard @BBL A1M"), I opened `general_purpose_hook.STL` the way Finder does (a macOS
open-file event). The new project's chat starts with nine rows, all "you, in 0.20mm Standard
@BBL A1M · 07:02", above "Opened general_purpose_hook.STL as a new project":

Sparse infill density 20% → 15%, Sparse infill pattern Cross Zag → Cross Hatch, Skeleton infill
density 20% → 15%, Skin infill density 20% → 15%, Type Normal (auto) → Tree (auto), First layer
0.36 mm → 0.5 mm, Outer wall 0.34 mm → 0.42 mm, Inherits profile 0.20mm Standard @BBL A1M → Empty,
print_settings_id HSW_Kabelhalter → Empty.

Screenshot of the captured chat: `phantom-edits-repro.png` (same folder).

## Why

lldb backtrace of every row: `MacOpenFiles` → `Plater::load_files` → `ShellController::take_opened_files`
→ `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter::release_project` → `drop_unsaved_edits` → `Tab::load_current_preset` →
`Plater::on_config_change` → `notify_project_state_changed(Settings)` → `record_settings_edits(report=true)`.

`release_project` (OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:2593) does two steps in this order:

1. `new_project(...)`. Orca's reset reports one "project replaced" change. The adapter treats
   that as "nothing in a new project is an edit" and silently records the current settings as the
   new baseline. At that moment the 3MF's embedded values are still in force, as unsaved edits on
   top of the system preset with the same name (that is how Orca loads them).
2. `drop_unsaved_edits` on the printer, process and filament tabs (Orca's Discard). This runs
   after the new-project transaction has closed, so it arrives as an ordinary settings change. The
   adapter compares it to the baseline from step 1 and publishes nine setting edits. The actor is
   Person because "Person" is the default for anything a tool did not start.

`ProjectPersistence::on_edit` attaches to the new project before storing, so the entries go into the
new chat. `ChangeRows.tsx` labels every non-agent entry "you".

Nothing actually changed for the person. The autosave hook saved the old project, embedded settings
included, before releasing it. The new project starts from the system preset, as every new project does.

**Which ways in are affected:**
- Finder open: run and confirmed.
- Home's Open… button and a drop on Home: these go through the same `take_opened_files` →
  `release_project` path (read from the code). I did not run them, because the Home page pauses its
  timers while hidden and Kenneth declined screen control.
- The `project_open` tool also calls `release_project` (OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:2557). From the
  code, its rows would be labelled "Agent" or with the external client's name. Not run.
- Home's "New project" button calls Orca's `new_project` without the discard step. Not checked.

**Side observation, not isolated.** In one of three launches, opening the 3MF itself at startup
produced the reverse rows (system values → the file's values, plus "Switched to Bambu PLA Basic
@BBL A1M") in the 3MF's own chat. A later launch with a fresh copy of the data folder produced none.
Orca's `load_project` wraps reset and load in one transaction, so I'd expect a 3MF opened in a
running app to stay silent. I did not test that: with `single_instance` off, a Finder-opened 3MF
starts a second app instance against the real data folder.

## Options

**1. Take the new baseline after the discard (host). Recommended.**
After `drop_unsaved_edits`, `release_project` records the settings baseline again without reporting
(`record_settings_edits(false)`), or runs the discard inside the new project's transaction.
- What the person sees: the new chat starts with "Opened general_purpose_hook.STL as a new
  project". The old file is not mentioned.
- Where it lives: about five lines in OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp. It belongs in C++ because whether
  OrcaSlicer state changed is the first strong reason in the page-first rule. It also fixes the tool path.
- Test: `tests/workspace/real_adapter_harness.cpp` already collects `m_edits`. Make the process tab
  dirty, call `release_project`, and assert that no Setting edit is published. Then make a real edit
  and assert that it is reported. Prove the test fails without the fix first.

**2. One line, credited to the file (host and page).**
Store one entry such as "Settings from Tape_4_3MF.3mf were put back" with no "you". This needs a
new kind or actor in the stored change log, the old project's name in the entry, and new wording in
`ChangeRows.tsx` plus a wording test.
- What the person sees: one line about a file they closed, at the top of a new project.
- Why not: they can't act on it, and Orca says nothing at this point either. It is only worth doing if
  Kenneth wants the "settings don't carry over" behaviour to be visible.

**3. Keep the rows, but in the old project's chat (host).**
Publish the rows before the project boundary.
- What the person sees: nine rows at the end of the old chat the next time they open it.
- Why not: the rows would be false there too. The saved file still holds those values, and
  reopening the file restores them.

**4. Hide them in the page.**
Drop setting rows that come before the first "Opened … as a new project" line.
- Why not: the stored log still holds nine false "person" edits. Any person edit also marks the
  active plan as needing reassessment (ProjectPersistence.cpp:150). That does no harm here only
  because a brand-new project has no plan yet. This hides a false record instead of not writing it.

## Should `print_settings_id` and "Empty" ever reach a row?

No. These keys record which preset this is (`inherits`, `print_settings_id`, `printer_settings_id`,
`filament_settings_id`, `compatible_*`); they are not print settings. `SettingsSupport.hpp` already
blocks `inherits` and `compatible_*` from tool writes, because "a different value breaks the preset".
The change log never consults that list, and the `*_settings_id` keys are not on it.
`preset_deltas_of` also falls back to the raw key when a setting has no label
(OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:212), and that is how `print_settings_id` appears.

"Empty" is the display for an empty value. It is fine for a G-code field someone cleared, and it
shows up here only because of the identity keys.

Suggestion: `record_settings_edits` should skip identity keys and keys with no label. That is a
host change next to the existing list. It is independent of options 1–4: option 1 alone already
removes these rows here, but the same keys could show up after other preset operations. It can go in
with option 1 or as its own follow-up.

2. Only after that does it discard those unsaved edits on each preset tab. The discard arrives as an ordinary settings change, so the adapter compares it to the starting point and publishes nine setting edits. They are marked as the person's because that is the default for anything a tool didn't start.

The new project gets these entries, and the page labels any edit not made by the agent "you". An lldb backtrace on every row confirmed this path. Nothing actually changed for the person: the old project had already been saved with its settings.

**Which ways of opening a file are affected:**

- **Home's Open… button and a drop on Home:** these call the same function, but I only confirmed that from the code. Kenneth declined screen control, and the hidden Home page doesn't run its timers, so I couldn't trigger them.
- **The `project_open` tool:** also calls `release_project`. From the code, its rows would be labelled "Agent" or with the client's name instead of "you". Not run.

**Options in the note:**
1. **Recommended: take the settings starting point again after the discard,** in the host (C++), about five lines in `release_project`. The new chat would start with "Opened … as a new project" and nothing else. The test goes in `tests/workspace/real_adapter_harness.cpp`, which already collects these edits.
2. **One line credited to the file,** such as "Settings from Tape_4_3MF.3mf were put back." This needs a change to the stored change log and new page wording. I don't recommend it: it's noise the person can't act on.
3. **Keep the rows, but in the old project's chat.** They would be false there too, because the saved file still holds those values.
4. **Hide the rows in the page only.** The stored log would still record nine edits by the person that never happened.

**`print_settings_id` and "Empty":** keys like this should never reach a row. They record which preset is in use; they are not print settings. On 2026-10-21 Kenneth found 4 Release builds and 56 clang processes on 12 cores, all mine, in one worktree. Every ninja ran at its default -j (cores + 2), so 4 × 14 = 56. He pointed out that the orphaned processes were the smaller problem. The bigger one was that I put that many builds there at all.

What I did wrong, in order of weight:
1. I treated builds as free on a machine other sessions build on too. I never passed `-j`. I saw load 33, then 76, and started more builds anyway.
2. I restarted the build three times to change its target list or to slip in a small target. Each restart cost a full set of jobs. Waiting for the running build and adding targets afterwards cost nothing.
3. I went against the brief ("reuse the existing build; another session may be building") by configuring a fresh full-app build for an optional live check.
4. I blamed the slowness on "other sessions" without counting my own processes. That is the plausible-story-instead-of-checking failure from CLAUDE.md.
5. Mechanism: `pkill -f "cmake --build <dir>"` kills only the wrapper. Its `ninja -C <dir>` child keeps compiling as an orphan. I never checked that a stop had worked.

**Why:** the machine is shared. My extra jobs slow every other session, and two ninjas in one build dir can leave its records inconsistent.

**How to apply:**
- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. Cap jobs with `-- -j4` (fewer when load is above the core count).
- Decide the full target list once. Never restart a build to change it.
- Run one build per dir as its own process group (`set -m`, then kill with `kill -- -<pgid>`). After any stop, confirm with `pgrep -fl "ninja.*<dir>"`.
- Ask before a full-app build that the task did not require.

Related: [[background-bash-timeout-kills-builds]], [[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]], [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

On 2026-10-21 Kenneth's Mac ran at load average 32 on 12 cores for over an hour. The cause was one Claude session (the "Show MCP edits without an agent" worktree session) that launched four `nohup cmake --build … --config Release` runs between 10:56 and 11:05 into the same build dir (`.claude/worktrees/mcp-external-edits/build/arm64`), three with identical target sets. Each ninja spawned ~12 clang jobs, so 56 clang processes fought over 12 cores and every build crawled. The session had gone idle at 11:13 with its work already committed, and the builds kept running as orphans (parent pid 1) because of nohup.

**Why:** a nohup'd build survives the Bash tool timeout (see [[background-bash-timeout-kills-builds]]), so re-launching "the build" after each timeout adds a build instead of resuming one. ninja does not lock the build dir; concurrent instances just duplicate work and thrash.

**How to apply:**
- Before any `nohup cmake --build`, run `pgrep -fl 'ninja -f' ` and `lsof -a -d cwd -p <pid>`; if a ninja already has that build dir as cwd, tail its log instead of starting another.
- Never launch the same target set twice; wait on the saved PID with `kill -0` (see [[pgrep-wait-loop-matches-itself]]).
- Before ending a turn with the task done, kill builds you started that nobody will read (`pkill -P <ninja pid>; kill <ninja pid>`), or say in the recap that one is still running and why.
- To find who owns a stray build: the ninja's stdout path (`lsof -p <pid> -d 1`) contains the Claude Code session id; `ps -o args= -p $(pgrep -f -- "--resume=<id>")` shows the app session's side-session-notes path.

**The fix** (`OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp` / `.hpp`, about 8 lines). When a file opens as a new project, `release_project` throws away the old project's unsaved preset values after the new project has already started. It now sets a flag, `m_dropping_released_edits`, while it does that. While the flag is set, the adapter quietly records the reset values as the new project's starting settings instead of publishing them as the person's edits. I gave it its own flag rather than reusing the calibration one, because other code reads `generating_calibration()`. The same change also fixes the agent's `project_open` tool, which goes through the same function.

**Test:** a new step in `tests/workspace/real_adapter_harness.cpp` makes the process preset dirty, releases the project, and checks two things: no setting edit is published, and a real edit made afterwards is still logged once.
